samples.text:
THE KIRANA PLAYBOOK
How neighbourhood grocery stores can modernise, keep their customers and beat the ten-minute apps
A book proposal by [Author name], retail consultant, Indore

OVERVIEW

Everyone says the kirana is finished. The ten-minute apps have arrived, the supermarket chains have the shelf space, and the owner's son would rather work in Pune. Walk into most neighbourhood stores at 8 pm and the story looks true: a handwritten udhaar register, three phones ringing with orders nobody is writing down, and a back room full of stock that has not moved since Diwali.

But the shops that are doing well look exactly the same from the street. The difference is inside. They know which 200 items earn their rent. They take WhatsApp orders on a fixed format and deliver them in a fixed window. They give credit to customers they can name and stop credit to those they cannot. None of this needed a loan, an app developer or a franchise.

The Kirana Playbook shows a neighbourhood grocery owner how to make those changes in his own shop, one at a time, in the order that pays for the next one.

That is the promise of the book in one sentence, and every chapter is built to keep it. It is not a book about the death of small retail or a celebration of it. It is a working manual for the person behind the counter, written by someone who has stood there with 140 of them.

Over [number] years, [Author name] has advised 140 kirana owners, most of them in Indore and the towns around it. The book turns that work into a sequence of changes a store owner can make without closing the shutter for a day. Count what actually sells. Cut dead stock. Set rules for credit. Take orders on WhatsApp without losing them. Price against the apps on the items where it matters, and ignore them where it does not. Then hand the business to a son or daughter in a form that runs on numbers instead of memory.

The angle no other book takes is the counter-level view. Books on Indian retail tend to be written for the companies that compete with kiranas, or for investors who want to understand them. Small-business books written in the US assume a shop that has a manager, a POS system and a bank that lends on cash flow. This book starts from the shop as it is: one owner, one or two helpers, a cash drawer, a UPI QR code stuck to the counter and customers who have bought there for fifteen years. Each chapter ends with a one-page checklist the owner can stick next to that QR code.

The voice is practical and direct. Each chapter opens inside a real shop situation drawn from the author's consulting files, with names and details changed and the owner's consent recorded. It then lays out the change, what it costs, and how long it took to pay back in the shops that tried it. Where the result varied, the book says so.

Format: approximately [60,000] words, 12 chapters, with checklists, simple record formats the owner can copy into a register, and a short glossary of the terms suppliers and distributors use. A Hindi edition is planned with the same structure. Manuscript delivery: [month, year], [number] months from contract.

TARGET READERSHIP

The primary reader is the owner of an independent neighbourhood grocery store in a Tier 2 or Tier 3 city who reads English for business, or whose son or daughter does. Typically he is 35 to 55, runs a store of 200 to 600 square feet, and has seen footfall drop since quick-commerce apps reached his area. He already buys practical business books, usually in paperback, usually after seeing a recommendation on YouTube or WhatsApp. [Market size: number of kirana stores in India and the share in Tier 2-3 cities, with source and year.]

The second reader is the next generation: the 22-to-30-year-old who has an MBA or a commerce degree, has come back to the family shop, and needs a plan the father will accept. This reader buys online, follows business creators on LinkedIn and Instagram, and is the most likely buyer of the English edition as a gift for the family.

The third group is the people who sell to kiranas and need them to survive: FMCG sales teams, distributors and the B2B ordering platforms. They buy in bulk for training. The author has worked with [number] such teams; a bulk-sales note follows in the marketing section.

These readers can be found and counted: through trader associations in each city, through FMCG distributor networks, and through the author's own audience of 38,000 LinkedIn followers, a large share of whom work in retail, distribution and FMCG.

COMPARABLE TITLES

The books below show that the same readers buy practical, owner-level business books, and that none of them yet speaks to the Indian neighbourhood store.

The E-Myth Revisited, Michael E. Gerber (HarperBusiness, 1995). Older than the market it proves, but still the book most small-business owners are handed first, and still sold in Indian airports and bookshops. It argues that owners must build systems instead of doing every job themselves. The Kirana Playbook makes the same argument for a shop where the system has to fit in a register and a WhatsApp group, not an operations manual.

Profit First, Mike Michalowicz (Portfolio, revised edition 2017) [COMP: verify edition year]. A cash-management method for owners who earn revenue but never see profit, popular with Indian founders on LinkedIn. Its bank-account method assumes US banking. The Playbook covers the same pain, working capital stuck in stock and credit, using the tools a kirana already has.

Jugaad Innovation, Navi Radjou, Jaideep Prabhu and Simone Ahuja (Jossey-Bass, 2012). Proved there is a readership for books on frugal Indian business ingenuity. It is written for corporate managers looking at small enterprises from outside. The Playbook is written from inside the shop, for the person running it.

[COMP: verify title, author, publisher, year: a 2022-2025 Indian business book on small retail, quick commerce or family-business succession, published by an Indian trade imprint.] This slot should show recent Indian demand for the subject. Two candidates are being checked against publisher catalogues before the proposal goes out; neither is listed here until confirmed.

Taken together, the comparable titles show readers who will pay for systems thinking and for Indian business stories. They also show the gap between them: no current trade book teaches a kirana owner, in his own terms, how to change the way his shop runs.

samples.brief: Blog article summarising Cal Newport's 'Deep Work' for an Indian edtech blog read by UPSC and CA aspirants studying at home; 5 key ideas, each with an example from a 10-hour study day in a shared flat; one critique; verdict on who should read the full book; English; 800-1,100 words; CTA: save the article and try one idea this week.
samples.text:
5 ideas from Deep Work every UPSC and CA aspirant should try before the next mock test

You put in ten hours at the desk yesterday. How many of them were real study, the kind where you could close the book and explain the chapter to someone else? If the honest answer is three, this book was written for your problem.

Deep Work by Cal Newport (Grand Central Publishing, 2016) argues one thing: the ability to focus without distraction on hard material is becoming rare, and so it is becoming valuable. Newport is a computer science professor, and he writes for office workers drowning in email. But his advice fits an aspirant in a shared flat even better, because your exam rewards almost nothing except focused hours.

Here are the five ideas worth taking from it, each tried on a real study day.

1. Deep work and shallow work are different jobs

Newport splits work into two kinds. Deep work is hard, focused effort that stretches your ability. Shallow work is everything you can do while distracted: replying, sorting, scrolling, re-reading notes you already know. He also cites research on what he calls attention residue: when you switch tasks, part of your mind stays on the last one, so you start the next one at less than full strength.

On your study day: Take a 10-hour day in a flat with three other aspirants. Two hours of it go to the Telegram current-affairs channel, the group discussion about which coaching notes are better, and making a fresh timetable. That is shallow work wearing a study costume. Tonight, write your day in two columns. Most aspirants find the deep column is shorter than they thought.

2. Pick a rhythm for depth, don't wait for the mood

Newport describes four ways people build deep work into their lives, from the monastic (cut off almost everything) to the journalistic (go deep whenever a gap appears). For most people he suggests the rhythmic way: the same time, every day, until it becomes a habit you no longer argue with.

On your study day: Your flatmates wake at different times and the kitchen is busiest at 8 am. Fix your first deep block at 6 to 8:30 am, before anyone is up, every day including Sunday. Ninety minutes of Indian Polity or Advanced Accounting at the same hour, daily, beats a heroic 14-hour Sunday.

3. Take breaks from focus, not breaks from distraction

Newport's most useful reversal: most of us treat the phone as the normal state and study as the interruption. He says do the opposite. Schedule the times you are allowed to go online, and stay offline outside them, even when you are bored. Boredom, he argues, is training: if you never let your mind sit with it, you lose the ability to hold your attention on one hard thing.

On your study day: Keep a paper slip on the desk with your next internet time written on it, say 11:00. Doubt about a GST provision at 10:20? Write it on the slip and keep going. At 11:00, check all of them in one go. You will find half of them answered themselves by then.

4. Judge every app by what it does for your goal

Newport does not ask you to hate social media. He asks you to treat each tool the way a craftsman treats tools: keep it only if its benefits to your main goal clearly outweigh its costs. He suggests a test: stop using a service for 30 days without announcing it, then ask whether those 30 days were worse and whether anyone noticed.

On your study day: List every app on your phone that you opened yesterday. For each, ask one question: does this help me clear Prelims or CA Inter this year? Instagram fails. The doubt-clearing group of your coaching batch may pass. Log out of the ones that fail for 30 days and see what you actually miss.

5. Plan every minute, then close the day on purpose

The last part of the book is about shrinking shallow work. Newport schedules every minute of his workday in blocks on paper, and redraws the plan when the day goes off track, which it often does. He ends each day with a shutdown ritual: check what is pending, plan tomorrow, then say a fixed phrase ("Shutdown complete") so the mind stops chewing on work.

On your study day: At 9:30 pm, spend ten minutes writing tomorrow's blocks, chapter by chapter, on one page. Then close the book and do not open the syllabus PDF in bed. When your flatmate starts discussing the cut-off at midnight, you already know what tomorrow holds and can go to sleep.

Where the book does not fit you

Deep Work was written for office workers who have a door they can close. They also have the money for what Newport calls a grand gesture, like renting a quiet room for a few weeks to finish a big project. In a shared flat with one table, a pressure cooker going off every morning and a family call every evening, the monastic options are not available. The book also leans on stories of famous writers and professors more than on data, so read the bigger claims as one professor's argument, not settled science. And it says little about sleep, food or the anxiety of a long exam cycle, which decide how many deep hours you can actually do.

Should you read the full book?

Read it if you have already tried timetables and they collapse by Wednesday. The chapters on rules (especially 3 and 4 above) give you a system, not a pep talk. Skip it if you already study in fixed blocks with your phone in another room; you are doing the book. Either way, save this article and try one idea this week. Start with the paper slip. It costs nothing and you will know by Sunday whether it works.

samples.brief: Brand manifesto for 'Chhaap', a Jaipur hand-block-print apparel label (Sanganer printers, natural dyes) launching a slow-fashion line for urban women 25-40; used as the 60-second launch-film voice-over and the About page; English with two or three Hindi words; 120-200 words; must pass the swap test against fast-fashion brands.
samples.text:
A new collection every Friday.
A bag of clothes by the door every month.
Nobody remembers buying them. Nobody knows who made them.

We got tired of clothes that ask nothing of anyone.

In Sanganer, a printer dips a carved wooden block in dye.
He sets it on the cloth and presses with the heel of his hand.
Lifts it. Moves one block along. Presses again.

We believe a print should show the hand that made it.
We believe the small shift where one block meets the next is the signature, so we leave it in.
We believe colour from natural dyes can be bright enough for a Monday meeting.
We believe a kurta should outlast the trend it was never part of.

So we will make less.
Every Chhaap piece is block-printed by hand in Sanganer, coloured with natural dyes.
No weekly drops.
Just clothes made dheere, for women who keep what they love.

Wear it for years.
Wear the hand that made it.

Chhaap. Made to leave a mark.

samples.brief: Name shortlist for a Bengaluru millet-snack D2C startup selling baked millet chips to office-goers 25-40 on Swiggy Instamart and its own site; 10 names across 3 territories, each with rationale, respelling, Hindi and Kannada meaning check and preliminary domain/handle/trademark flags; English; 500-800 words; recommend the top 2.
samples.text:
NAME SHORTLIST: BAKED MILLET CHIPS, BENGALURU

1. Brief recap

Product: baked millet chips, sold on Swiggy Instamart and our own site.
Buyer: office-goers aged 25-40 in Bengaluru, snacking at the desk or on the way home.
Positioning in one line: the 4 pm snack you don't have to feel bad about.
Languages to check: English, Hindi, Kannada.
Names to stay clear of: Kurkure, Soulfull, Slurrp Farm, Millet Amma [client to confirm the full competitor list].
No-gos: clever spellings people cannot search on Instamart; anything that sounds like diet food.

2. Territories

A. Grain-first: names the millet, so the health claim does the work.
B. The office moment: names when and where it is eaten, not what is in it.
C. Short and coined: a sound that is easy to say, search and brand, with a local root.

3. Shortlist

Territory A: grain-first

Siri (SIH-ree). From siridhanya, the Kannada word for millets; in Kannada siri also means prosperity. Fits because it is local pride in one word. Hindi check: fails. Siri paya is a meat dish (goat head and trotters), a bad association for a veg snack in the Hindi belt. English: Apple's assistant will bury it in search.

Navane (nuh-VUH-nay). Kannada for foxtail millet. Fits a Bengaluru-first launch and sounds warm. Hindi: no meaning, but non-Kannada buyers will spell it navane, navanay or nawane. Fails the spell-from-hearing test.

Jola Co. (JO-laa). Jola is jowar in Kannada. Hindi ears hear jhola, the cloth bag, which is a friendly, desi association. Risk: "Co." names feel like a grocery store, not a snack.

Territory B: the office moment

Four O'Clock (for uh-KLOCK). Names the slump every desk worker knows. Fits because it sells the occasion, and it works in every language with no meaning to check. Hindi and Kannada: neutral, already said in English in both. Risk: a common phrase, so domain and trademark are crowded.

Breakout (BRAKE-out). The meeting room, and the crack of a chip. Hindi and Kannada: no meaning. Risk: a common English word used by many brands; weak as a mark.

Standup (STAND-up). The morning team meeting, and stand-up comedy: a snack with a sense of humour. Hindi and Kannada: no meaning. Risk: reads as a comedy brand before a food brand.

Millet Byte (MIL-it bite). A pun for Bengaluru's tech offices. Fails the radio test: half the people who hear it will type "bite". Descriptive, so weak as a trademark.

Territory C: short and coined

Tindi (TIN-dee). Kannada for snack or tiffin, said in every Bengaluru office. Fits because it is the word the buyer already uses. Hindi: tinda is a gourd, close but not negative, and most Hindi speakers will hear it as new. Risk: generic in Kannada, so harder to register as a mark.

Ragaa (ruh-GAA). Ragi plus raga, the Hindi and Kannada word for melody. Pleasant in both languages. Fails the spell-from-hearing test: raga, raaga and ragaa all look right.

Kodo (KO-doh). Kodo millet is known by this name in Hindi; in Kannada kodu means "give", which suits a pack people share. Two syllables, one obvious spelling. Risk: if the chips contain kodo millet, the name may be treated as descriptive at registration.

4. Availability flags (preliminary, needs attorney clearance)

None of these has been searched yet; the notes below are risk estimates to guide the searches, not results.

Siri: .com and handles almost certainly taken; class 30 search needed.
Navane: domain likely open; handle unknown; class 30 search needed.
Jola Co.: domain unknown; check class 30 and 29 for "Jola".
Four O'Clock: exact .com likely taken; try .in and a modifier; class 30 likely crowded.
Breakout: domain and handles likely taken; many marks across classes.
Standup: domain likely taken; check class 30 and 41.
Millet Byte: domain possibly open; descriptive, weak mark.
Tindi: domain and handles likely used by restaurants; class 30 and 43 search needed.
Ragaa: domain possibly open; check class 30.
Kodo: domain likely taken overseas; check .in and handle variants; class 30 search needed.

5. Recommendation

1. Four O'Clock. It is the only name that sells the moment of eating instead of the ingredient, and it travels to Pune or Hyderabad without a translation. Risk: trademark and domain crowding. Next step: attorney search in class 30 first; if blocked, test "Four O'Clock Millet" as the full mark.

2. Kodo. Short, real, easy to spell from hearing, with a warm Kannada echo. Risk: descriptiveness if kodo millet is in the recipe. Next step: ask the attorney before any design work.

Test both: say each aloud to 20 office-goers, ask them to type it into a phone, and count how many spell it right.

samples.brief: About-page brand story for 'Sahyadri Sun', a Nashik family farm that sold raisins to mandi traders for 20 years and now sells sulphur-free raisins direct to urban health-conscious buyers; facts supplied: 2019 price crash at the Pimpalgaon mandi, 14 partner farms, residue tests on every batch; English; 400-600 words plus a 60-word short version; CTA to shop the trial pack.
samples.text:
OUR STORY

In the spring of 2019, my father drove our raisins to the Pimpalgaon mandi, as he had every season for twenty years. The trader opened a box, rubbed a few raisins between his fingers and named a price. It was [2019 price per kg, client to confirm], less than it had cost us to grow, dry and pack them. There was no other buyer that day. He sold, and drove back to the farm in silence.

That was the year we stopped selling to the mandi.

What was wrong

For two decades we grew grapes on our land outside Nashik, dried them into raisins and handed them to a trader. We never met the people who ate them. The price was set in the mandi, by the trader, on the day. If it rained at the wrong time or the market was flooded, we took what we were offered.

The people at the other end were losing too. Many raisins in the market are bright gold because they have been treated with sulphur to keep that colour. Buyers had no way of knowing what was on them, where they came from or how long they had sat in a godown. You paid for a colour, not a farm.

What we decided

We decided to dry our raisins without sulphur, test every batch, and sell them ourselves to the families who would eat them.

It cost us. Sulphur-free raisins are darker, and the traders who had bought from us for years would not take them at a good price. The first season we sold a fraction of what we used to, mostly to friends and relatives in Pune and Mumbai, packed on our own veranda. The testing alone costs us [cost per batch test, client to confirm] every time.

But the families who tried them came back, and told their friends.

What exists now

Sahyadri Sun is now 14 farms. The other 13 are neighbours who grow and dry the way we do, and sell through us instead of the mandi. Every batch from every farm is tested for pesticide residue at [lab name] before it is packed, and the report is [where customers can see it: on the website, by batch number, client to confirm]. If a batch fails, it does not go out.

Our raisins are brown, not gold. They taste of the grape they came from. And you know exactly which farm and which batch you are eating, because it is printed on the pack.

Your part in it

Every pack you buy goes straight from the farm to your kitchen, with no mandi in between. The price we get is a price we can grow on, and the 14 farms that grow for us can keep doing it the honest way.

Start with the trial pack. Taste the difference sulphur makes, and see the test report for your batch.

[Shop the trial pack]


SHORT VERSION (60 words)

For twenty years our family sold raisins to traders at the Pimpalgaon mandi. In 2019 prices crashed below our cost, and we stopped. Now 14 Nashik farms dry raisins without sulphur, test every batch for residue and sell straight to you. Darker than you are used to, and honest about where they come from. Try the trial pack.

ONE-SENTENCE VERSION

Sahyadri Sun is 14 Nashik farms that left the mandi after the 2019 price crash to sell sulphur-free, residue-tested raisins straight to the families who eat them.

samples.brief: Voice and tone guide for 'TokriNow', a Lucknow-based quick-commerce grocery app serving Hindi-belt cities; covers app microcopy, WhatsApp order updates and Instagram; English plus Hinglish (Roman) rules; 3 voice traits, 6 tone situations including a late delivery and a refund, a 20-row vocabulary table, 6 before/after rewrites; 1,000-1,500 words.
samples.text:
TOKRINOW VOICE AND TONE GUIDE
Version 1.0. Owner: [Brand lead name], Lucknow. Last updated: [date]. Review every six months.

1. Who this is for

Anyone who writes words a TokriNow customer will read: app screens and buttons, WhatsApp order updates, push notifications, and Instagram posts and replies. If you are a freelancer, an agency writer or a new hire on customer support, read sections 2, 3 and 7 before your first draft. When the guide and your instinct disagree, follow the guide and tell the owner.

2. Our voice: three traits

Our customers are families in Lucknow, Kanpur, Varanasi and other Hindi-belt cities, ordering milk, sabzi and atta for today. They talk to us the way they talk to the kirana bhaiya who knows their order. Our voice is that bhaiya on his best day.

Trait 1: Apna, not over-friendly
We sound familiar and respectful, like someone from the mohalla. We always say aap, never tum. We don't use slang, nicknames or forced jokes.
Do: "Aapka order nikal gaya hai. 14 min mein pahunchega."
Don't: "Yo! Your goodies are zooming your way, fam!"

Trait 2: Clear, not clever
Every message answers one question: what is happening and when. Times, amounts and next steps come first. Wordplay is allowed on Instagram, never in an order update.
Do: "Rider 2 km door hai. Pahunchne mein lagbhag 8 min."
Don't: "Your tokri is on a mission. Stay tuned for the magic!"

Trait 3: Owns it, doesn't hide
When we get something wrong, we say what went wrong, say sorry once, and say what we are doing about it. We never blame the rider, the weather or "technical issues" without detail.
Do: "Aapka order 20 min late hai. Hamari galti hai. Delivery fee wapas kar di hai."
Don't: "Due to unforeseen circumstances, there may be a slight delay. We regret the inconvenience."

3. Tone by situation

The voice stays the same. The tone moves with the customer's mood.

Order placed (routine): short and calm. "Order mil gaya. Packing shuru, 14 min mein aapke ghar."

Late delivery: lead with the new time, then the reason, then what we did. No emoji, no exclamation mark. "Aapka order 15 min late hoga. Hamare rider ki bike kharab ho gayi, doosra rider nikal chuka hai. Is order ki delivery fee hum le nahi rahe."

Item out of stock: say it before the customer finds out at the door, and give a choice. "Amul Taaza 1 litre khatam ho gaya. Mother Dairy 1 litre bhej dein, same price? Haan / Nahi, hata dein."

Refund: the amount, the method and the date, in that order. Calm and exact. "₹186 ka refund shuru ho gaya hai. 3-5 working din mein aapke UPI account mein aa jayega. Refund ID: [ID]."

Complaint on Instagram: reply in public once, then move it to DM. Never argue in comments. "Bahut sorry, ye nahi hona chahiye tha. Aapko DM kiya hai, order number bhej dijiye, aaj hi theek karte hain."

Festival or celebration: warmer, one emoji allowed, still clear about the offer and the date. "Dhanteras ki shubhkamnayein 🪔 Aaj raat 10 baje tak dry fruits par 15% off."

4. Vocabulary

Use | Avoid | Why
order | parcel, package | customers call it their order
rider | delivery boy, executive | respect for the person
sabzi | veggies, greens | the word our customers use
atta | flour | same
doodh / milk | dairy beverages | plain words win
min (in app) | mins, minutes | fits the ETA chip
lagbhag 10 min | in a jiffy, superfast | give a number
aap | tum, tu, dost | respect, always
refund | money-back, reversal | one fixed term
wapas kar diya | processed, initiated | says what happened
galti | inconvenience | owns the mistake
sorry (once) | sincerest apologies | one sorry is enough
offer | deal of the century, loot | no hype
khatam ho gaya | currently unavailable | plain and honest
chuniye | kindly select | direct
TokriNow | Tokri Now, Tokrinow, TN | fixed brand spelling
Tokri Pass | membership, subscription | fixed product name
delivery fee | convenience charge, handling fee | say what it pays for
Haan / Nahi (buttons) | Yes / No in Hinglish flows | match the message language
aapke ghar | your doorstep | how people actually say it

5. Language and mechanics

Spelling: Indian English. Colour, cheque, centre.
Money: ₹ with no space, no decimals unless needed: ₹186, not Rs. 186.00. Large numbers in lakh and crore.
Time: 12-hour, lower case: 7:40 pm. ETAs as "14 min".
Hinglish script: Roman only on WhatsApp, push and Instagram. Devanagari only in the Hindi app setting, never mixed with Roman in one message.
Fixed Hinglish spellings: hai (not h), nahi (not nahin or nai), kya (not kia), aapka (not apka), dijiye (not dijie), theek (not thik).
English words that stay English in Hinglish: order, delivery, rider, refund, UPI, cart, offer, app, slot, OTP.
Emoji: none in app microcopy, errors, delays or refunds. Maximum one in a WhatsApp update or Instagram caption.
Exclamation marks: maximum one per message, never in an apology.
Capitals: sentence case everywhere, including buttons. Never full caps for emphasis.
Names: greet by first name only if the customer has saved it; never guess gender.

6. Before and after

1. App, empty cart
Before: "Oops! Your cart is feeling lonely. Add some yummy items now!"
After: "Cart khaali hai. Roz ka saamaan yahan se jodiye: doodh, sabzi, atta."
What changed: removed the fake emotion and the exclamation marks; gave the next action.

2. WhatsApp, late delivery
Before: "Dear Customer, due to unforeseen circumstances your order may be delayed. We regret the inconvenience caused."
After: "Aapka order 15 min late hoga. Rider ki bike kharab hui, doosra rider nikal chuka hai. Delivery fee wapas kar di hai."
What changed: a number instead of "may be delayed", a real reason, and what we did about it.

3. WhatsApp, refund
Before: "Your refund has been initiated and will reflect in your account as per bank timelines."
After: "₹186 ka refund shuru ho gaya. 3-5 working din mein UPI account mein aa jayega. Refund ID: [ID]."
What changed: amount, method and date up front; "bank timelines" replaced with a range.

4. App, payment failed
Before: "Transaction failed. Error code 402."
After: "Payment nahi hua. Paise kate hain to 48 ghante mein wapas aa jayenge. Dobara try karein ya cash on delivery chuniye."
What changed: answered the customer's real worry (was money taken?) and gave two ways forward.

5. Instagram, complaint reply
Before: "We are sorry for the inconvenience. Please DM us your details and our team will look into it."
After: "Bahut sorry, sabzi kharab nikli, ye nahi hona chahiye tha. Aapko DM kiya hai, order number bhejiye, aaj hi refund karte hain."
What changed: named the problem, said what we will do, and gave a time.

6. Instagram, offer post
Before: "LOOT LO!!! Biggest sale EVER on groceries!!! Hurry!!!"
After: "Is Sunday 10 baje tak doodh aur atta par ₹30 off. Order karte waqt code SUNDAY30 lagaiye."
What changed: removed caps and hype, added the exact saving, deadline and code.

7. Quick checklist before you submit

Does the message say what is happening and when, in the first line?
Did you use aap, and the fixed Hinglish spellings?
Is there one script only (Roman or Devanagari)?
In a delay, refund or error: is there no emoji and no exclamation mark?
Is there a number (time, amount, date) where the customer needs one?
If we made a mistake, did we say sorry once and say what we did?
Is every product and brand name spelled as in the vocabulary table?
Would the kirana bhaiya say it this way to a regular customer?

[Company name] COMPANY PROFILE: 8 PAGES
Word budget per page shown in brackets. Language: plain English for buyers who read English as a second language.

PAGE 1: COVER [budget 15 words, used 14]

Precision CNC parts for automotive and pump makers.

BHOJAN GHAR: BUSINESS PLAN FOR A THIRD KITCHEN, PATNA
Sections: Executive summary, Market analysis, Funding request
Prepared for: [Branch name], [Public-sector bank]. Prepared by: [Promoter name(s)]. Date: [date].
All amounts in Indian rupees. Figures marked [CLIENT TO CONFIRM] are to be replaced from the books or vendor quotations before submission; every total below is recalculated from the lines above it.

1. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Bhojan Ghar is a delivery-only food brand in Patna, cooking home-style meals [menu summary: CLIENT TO CONFIRM] from two kitchens at [locality 1] and [locality 2]. Customers order through Swiggy, Zomato and our own channels, and we deliver within the delivery zones of each kitchen.

Last financial year, Bhojan Ghar earned revenue of Rs 1.90 crore at an EBITDA margin of 11%, which is EBITDA of Rs 20.9 lakh. 62% of orders came through Swiggy and Zomato; the other 38% came through [direct channels: phone, WhatsApp, own website: CLIENT TO CONFIRM].

The two kitchens average Rs 95 lakh of revenue each. Each kitchen can only serve customers within a limited delivery radius, so the main constraint on growth is distance, not demand. A third kitchen in [target locality] will reach customers our current kitchens cannot serve within delivery time.

We request a term loan of Rs 40 lakh to set up the third kitchen. The total project cost is Rs 50 lakh: Rs 40 lakh from the bank (80%) and Rs 10 lakh from the promoters (20%). The loan will be repaid in 60 monthly instalments after a 6-month moratorium.

Repayment comes from the cash the whole business generates. On the assumptions in section 3, combined EBITDA covers the loan's debt service 3.7 times in year 1 and 3.1 times in year 2, before tax and any existing loan repayments [existing borrowings: CLIENT TO CONFIRM].

2. MARKET ANALYSIS

2.1 Who buys

Our customers order a full meal for one or two people, mostly at lunch and dinner. From our order data, the main groups are [CLIENT TO CONFIRM from order data, e.g. working professionals, students living away from home, and families ordering on weekends]. They want food that tastes like a home meal at a price they can pay several times a week.

2.2 How big the market is

We size the market bottom-up, from what our own kitchens already do, rather than from a share of a national figure.

- Each existing kitchen earns Rs 95 lakh a year (Rs 1.90 crore across two kitchens).
- At an average order value of [Rs AOV: CLIENT TO CONFIRM], that is about [annual orders = 95 lakh / AOV] orders per kitchen per year.
- The third kitchen's delivery zone covers [number] households and [number] hostels and offices [source: CLIENT TO CONFIRM, e.g. ward data or aggregator zone report, with year].

Wider market figures to add with source and year:
- [Online food delivery orders in Patna per month: source, year]
- [Growth of online food ordering in Bihar or Tier 2 cities: source, year]

2.3 How customers buy now

Most of our customers find us on Swiggy and Zomato: 62% of our orders last year came through them. The aggregators bring reach, but each order carries a commission of [commission %: from Swiggy and Zomato contracts]. The 38% of orders that come directly carry no commission, which is why growing direct orders is part of the plan for the new kitchen.

2.4 Competitors

Customers in our delivery zones choose between:
- Local restaurants that also deliver through Swiggy and Zomato, such as [names of 2-3 local competitors: CLIENT TO CONFIRM].
- National delivery brands, such as Rebel Foods' Faasos and Behrouz Biryani, where they deliver in Patna [CLIENT TO CONFIRM presence in our zones].
- Home tiffin services, which are cheaper but offer a fixed menu and no on-demand ordering.

2.5 Where Bhojan Ghar fits

National brands sell fast food and biryani. Tiffin services sell a fixed daily meal. Bhojan Ghar sells home-style meals on demand, with [differentiator: CLIENT TO CONFIRM, e.g. menu, price point, delivery time]. Our 11% EBITDA margin on Rs 1.90 crore of revenue shows the model already makes money at two kitchens.

3. FUNDING REQUEST

3.1 The ask

Term loan: Rs 40 lakh.
Purpose: to set up and run Bhojan Ghar's third kitchen at [address].
Tenure: 66 months: 6-month moratorium (interest paid monthly), then 60 equal monthly instalments.
Security: [primary security on kitchen equipment and collateral: CLIENT TO CONFIRM; CGTMSE cover if eligible].

3.2 Cost of project and means of finance

Cost of project (Rs lakh)
Kitchen equipment (cooking range, refrigeration, exhaust, utensils): 18.0
Civil work and fit-out (gas line, fire safety, drainage): 11.0
Rent deposit: 4.5
Licences (FSSAI, fire NOC, trade licence), billing software and IT: 2.5
Launch marketing, first three months: 4.0
Working capital margin, first three months: 10.0
Total cost of project: 50.0

Means of finance (Rs lakh)
Term loan from bank: 40.0 (80%)
Promoters' contribution: 10.0 (20%)
Total: 50.0

Each line above is a planning figure to be replaced by vendor quotations and the rent agreement [CLIENT TO CONFIRM]. If a line changes, the promoters' contribution absorbs the difference so the loan request stays at Rs 40 lakh.

3.3 How the loan will be repaid

Assumptions:
1. The two existing kitchens hold last year's revenue (Rs 1.90 crore) and EBITDA margin (11%). No growth is assumed for them.
2. The third kitchen reaches 70% of the existing kitchens' average revenue in year 1 (Rs 66.5 lakh) and 100% in year 2 (Rs 95 lakh).
3. The third kitchen's EBITDA margin is 8% in year 1, because of launch costs, and 11% in year 2, matching the existing kitchens.
4. Interest rate of 10% a year [CLIENT TO CONFIRM with the bank's sanctioned rate].
5. The order mix stays at 62% through aggregators.

samples.brief: Feasibility report for the owners of a Surat saree manufacturer on whether to sell direct on marketplaces or stay wholesale-only; client data supplied: last-year wholesale revenue Rs 6.2 crore at 11% net margin, a 3-month marketplace pilot of 300 orders with a 14% return rate and Rs 410 average fulfilment cost per order; English; 900-1,300 words; three findings, three recommendations with owners and timelines.
samples.text:
SHOULD WE SELL SAREES DIRECT ON MARKETPLACES?
Feasibility report for the owners of [Company name], Surat
Prepared by: [Consultant name]. Date: October 2026.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The question: should [Company name] start selling sarees directly to customers on online marketplaces, or stay a wholesale-only business?

The answer: not yet, and not instead of wholesale. The three-month pilot shows that online selling is possible, but it does not yet show that it is profitable. Wholesale should stay the core business. Online selling should get one more structured test, with clear targets, before any money or people move away from wholesale.

Top findings:
1. 300 orders in three months is a test, not a channel. At about 100 orders a month, online sales are a very small fraction of the wholesale business, which earned Rs 6.2 crore last year.
2. Fulfilment and returns cost at least Rs 477 for every saree a customer keeps. Each order cost Rs 410 to fulfil, and 14% of orders came back.
3. The return rate decides whether online selling can ever pay. Every change of a few points in returns moves the cost per kept saree by tens of rupees, and we do not yet know why customers returned.

Recommendations:
1. Keep wholesale as the core business, with no cut in capacity or staff. Owner: [Managing partner]. From now.
2. Run a six-month second pilot with targets and full cost tracking, and decide at the end. Owner: [E-commerce lead]. November 2026 to April 2027.
3. Attack the causes of returns before the second pilot starts. Owner: [Production and catalogue head]. By 15 November 2026.

INTRODUCTION AND SCOPE

The owners asked whether the company should add direct marketplace selling to its wholesale business, or stay wholesale-only. This report compares the two using the company's own data.

In scope: last year's wholesale results, the three-month marketplace pilot, and the cost of fulfilling and returning online orders.
Out of scope: starting the company's own website, opening retail stores, and changes to the product range.

METHOD AND DATA

All figures come from the company's records:
- Wholesale revenue last financial year: Rs 6.2 crore, at a net margin of 11% (net profit of about Rs 68.2 lakh).
- Marketplace pilot, [pilot months, 2026]: 300 orders, a 14% return rate (42 orders returned), and an average fulfilment cost of Rs 410 per order.

Limits of the data:
- The pilot covers only three months and one season. It may not represent a full year, especially the wedding and festival months.
- We do not yet have the average online selling price, the marketplace commission, the return shipping charge, or the share of returned sarees that could be resold. These are marked as data needed below. Without them, we can show the minimum cost of online selling, not its full profit.

FINDINGS

Finding 1: 300 orders in three months is a test, not a channel

The pilot averaged about 100 orders a month, or three to four a day. The wholesale business, at Rs 6.2 crore a year, moves [wholesale units per month] sarees a month. Even if the pilot doubled every quarter, online selling would stay a small part of the business for at least a year.

What it means for the decision: online selling cannot replace any wholesale volume in the near term. The real question is whether it can add profit on top of wholesale, not whether it can replace it.

Finding 2: Fulfilment and returns cost at least Rs 477 for every saree a customer keeps

The 300 pilot orders cost Rs 1.23 lakh to fulfil (300 x Rs 410). Of those orders, 42 came back, so customers kept 258 sarees. Spread across the sarees that were kept, fulfilment cost Rs 477 per kept saree (Rs 1,23,000 / 258).

This is a minimum. It does not include the marketplace commission, return shipping, or the cost of sarees that come back damaged or unsellable [data needed from the marketplace settlement reports].

What it means for the decision: for a saree sold online to be worth more than the same saree sold wholesale, it must earn at least Rs 477 more per piece, plus commission and return costs. Wholesale already earns an 11% net margin with none of these costs.

Finding 3: The return rate decides whether online selling can ever pay

Using the pilot's fulfilment cost of Rs 410 per order:
- At 8% returns, fulfilment costs Rs 446 per kept saree.
- At 14% returns (the pilot), Rs 477.
- At 20% returns, Rs 513.

These are fulfilment costs only. Each return also brings back a saree that may need repacking, may be damaged, or may sit unsold. So the true cost of a higher return rate is larger than these numbers show.

We do not yet know why 42 customers sent their sarees back. The marketplace return reasons for the pilot [data needed] will show whether the cause is colour mismatch between photo and fabric, damage in transit, size or blouse-piece issues, or simple change of mind. The first three can be fixed by the company; the last cannot.

What it means for the decision: until the main return reasons are known and reduced, scaling up online selling would scale up the losses on returns.

ANALYSIS AND OPTIONS

Option A: Stay wholesale-only. Keeps the proven 11% margin and avoids new costs. The risk is that the company has no direct relationship with end customers if wholesale buyers start sourcing elsewhere or selling online themselves.

Option B: Move a large share of production to marketplaces now. Higher prices per saree are possible online, but the pilot shows high fulfilment and return costs and very low volume. This option puts the 11% wholesale margin at risk for an unproven gain.

Option C: Keep wholesale as the core, and run a second, structured online pilot. Costs little more than the first pilot, protects wholesale, and answers the open questions with data. This is the option we recommend.

RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Keep wholesale as the core business (from Findings 1 and 2)
No cut in wholesale capacity, staff or buyer relationships while online selling is tested.
Owner: [Managing partner]. Timeline: from now. Cost: none.

2. Run a six-month second pilot with targets, then decide (from Findings 1 and 2)
Sell 30 best-selling designs on one marketplace. Track every cost per order: selling price, commission, fulfilment, return shipping and unsellable returns. Go further only if, by April 2027, the pilot reaches [target orders per month] and each kept saree earns at least [target amount] more than the same saree sold wholesale.
Owner: [E-commerce lead]. Timeline: November 2026 to April 2027, review in May 2027. Cost: [pilot budget].

3. Attack the causes of returns before the second pilot (from Finding 3)
Pull the return reasons for all 42 pilot returns. Reshoot product photos in daylight with a colour reference card, add fabric, length and blouse-piece details to every listing, and test the packaging for transit damage. Target: a return rate below 10% in the second pilot.
Owner: [Production and catalogue head]. Timeline: by 15 November 2026. Cost: [photography and packaging cost].

The owners can decide today on recommendation 1. Recommendations 2 and 3 give them the data to decide on online selling in May 2027, with the wholesale business protected in the meantime.

samples.brief: Bylined article for the CFO of a Mumbai mid-size NBFC, for a BFSI trade publication, arguing that co-lending partnerships with banks fail at collections rather than at origination; draws on the CFO's account of a 2024 partnership that was paused; English; 800-1,100 words; no product or company mention outside a 2-line bio. || WRITER NOTE: The exemplar brief gives only the thesis and that a 2024 partnership was paused; the first-hand specifics (figures, fee structure, reason for the pause) are left as visible [CFO to confirm] placeholders for the executive interview.
samples.text:
Co-lending partnerships don't fail at origination. They fail at collections.

By [CFO name]

In [month] 2024, we paused a co-lending partnership with a bank [number] months after the first disbursement. On paper, it was working. The loans had been approved under a credit policy both sides had signed off. Disbursements had hit the plan. The early portfolio looked clean. What stopped us was a spreadsheet from our collections team showing [number] accounts that were current in our books and overdue in the bank's. [CFO to confirm the figures and timeline.]

Nobody had argued about who to lend to. We had argued, for months, about what happens after a borrower misses an instalment.

That is the pattern I now see across the industry. When co-lending partnerships between banks and NBFCs stall, the post-mortem usually blames origination: the bank's credit team was too slow, the two credit policies did not match, the approval system rejected good files. Those problems are real, but they are solvable and usually solved in the first quarter. The partnerships that fail tend to fail later, at collections, where the two lenders' incentives, systems and rules come apart. If you are negotiating a co-lending agreement, that is the part of the contract that deserves most of your time.

Origination is where the two sides already agree

Under the co-lending framework the Reserve Bank of India set out in November 2020, the NBFC keeps at least 20% of each loan on its own books and the bank takes the rest. In most arrangements, both lenders' credit teams approve each borrower against a policy they agreed in advance. By the time a loan is disbursed, both have looked at the same file and said yes.

This is why origination problems show up early and get fixed early. A credit-policy mismatch appears in the first hundred files. The approval delays are visible in turnaround reports every week. Both sides have a shared interest in getting good loans out of the door, and both can see the same data while doing it.

The counter-argument is fair: some partnerships do die at origination, usually when the bank's credit appetite turns out to be much narrower than the NBFC expected. But those partnerships rarely reach the point of having a portfolio to collect. The expensive failures are the ones that grow a book first.

Collections is where the incentives split

In most co-lending arrangements, the NBFC does all of the collection work on a loan in which it holds a minority share. The field visits, the calls, the reminders and the restructuring conversations are ours. The bank carries most of the credit risk but has no presence in the borrower's district.

That arrangement only works if the servicing fee pays for the work collections actually needs. A flat fee calculated on the outstanding book pays the same whether a portfolio is perfectly current or a fifth of it is overdue. When stress arrives, the cost of collecting rises sharply and the fee does not. The NBFC is then spending its own money to protect a loan that is mostly someone else's.

In our 2024 partnership, [CFO to confirm: how the servicing fee was structured, and how collection costs moved once overdue accounts began to rise].

The two lenders see the same loan differently

The more damaging problem is that the two lenders often do not agree on whether a borrower has paid.

A borrower in a small town may pay a field officer in cash on the 6th. The officer deposits it, the NBFC's system marks the instalment paid, and the money reaches the shared escrow account a day or two later. The bank's core banking system, meanwhile, has already counted the loan as overdue. Multiply that by a few hundred accounts, and the two lenders are reporting different overdue numbers for the same portfolio. One side's early-warning list becomes the other side's dispute.

Once that happens, every collections meeting turns into a reconciliation meeting. Staff on both sides spend their week matching receipts instead of talking to borrowers. Trust erodes faster than the portfolio does. In our case, that, more than any credit loss, is what made both sides agree to pause [CFO to confirm].

Nobody owns the borrower who is struggling

The third failure is a decision gap. When a borrower in genuine difficulty needs a restructured schedule, the NBFC's branch manager knows the family and the business. The bank has the larger exposure and the final say. If the agreement does not say who decides, how fast, and on what terms, the decision waits. A borrower who could have been saved with a three-month adjustment becomes a non-performing account while the two lenders exchange emails.

What to settle before the first disbursement

If I were negotiating a co-lending agreement today, I would not sign until four things were written into it:

1. One definition of overdue. Agree when a payment counts as received, including cash collected in the field, and make both systems use that date.
2. Daily reconciliation, not monthly. A shared report of every instalment received, matched by both sides every working day.
3. A servicing fee that follows the work. Part fixed, part linked to amounts recovered on overdue accounts, so the collecting lender is paid more when collecting is harder.
4. A named decision-maker for restructuring on each side, with a fixed number of days to respond.

None of these is complicated. They are just easy to leave for later, because at signing time everyone is focused on how many loans the partnership will book.

Our paused partnership taught us that the loan desk was never the problem. The collections desk was, and the conversation we should have had before the first loan went out. [CFO to confirm whether the partnership has since restarted, and on what terms.]

[CFO name] is Chief Financial Officer of [NBFC name], a Mumbai-based non-banking financial company that lends to [borrower segment]. [One line on prior role, e.g. previous finance or risk position.]

How a Nagpur pharma distributor got 93% of its reps logging daily visits in 10 weeks

SNAPSHOT
Customer: [Distributor name], pharma distributor, Nagpur
Team: 120 medical reps
Challenge: only 41% of reps logged their visits on a given day, and expense claims took 9 days to process.
Solution: [Product], a field-sales tracking app, with offline mode for rural beats.
Results: daily visit logging rose from 41% to 93% of reps in 10 weeks; expense-claim processing fell from 9 days to 3.

THE CUSTOMER AND THE CHALLENGE
[Distributor name] sells medicines out of Nagpur through 120 medical reps, who spend their working days visiting doctors and chemists across their beats. Visit data was what the sales head, [Name], used to run the team: who had been called on, which beats had gone quiet, where the next call should go.

The data was thin. On a given day, 41% of reps logged their visits, about 49 of 120. That left roughly 71 reps whose day [Name] could not see. When a month came in slow, he could not tell whether the market was soft or whether a beat had simply not been covered.

Expense claims were the second drag. A claim took 9 days to process, so a rep who had spent on travel for a week waited more than a week to be paid back, and whoever approved the claim had few logged visits to check it against.

WHY THEY CHOSE [PRODUCT]
Before deciding, [Name]'s team looked at [alternatives considered: confirm with the client]. What settled it, in [Name]'s words: "[the deciding reason, one sentence from the interview]". The requirement was plain: an app reps would open every working day, with visits and expense claims in one place so that the second job supported the first.

IMPLEMENTATION
The rollout ran for 10 weeks, starting with [pilot group and start date: confirm]. Reps installed [Product] on their own phones, logged each visit as it ended, and filed expense claims from the same app, so an approver saw a claim next to the visits behind it.

The first real problem came from the rural beats. Network coverage there is patchy. A rep who finished a call in a village often could not save it on the spot, and by evening the entry was either rushed or skipped. The reps dropping out of the data were the ones working the longest routes.

The fix was offline mode. The app now saves each visit on the phone and sends it to the server the next time the phone finds a network. A rep no longer waits for signal to finish a call, and a late entry stopped meaning a missing visit. With that in place, the rural beats started logging like the rest, and the share of reps logging each day kept climbing through the remaining weeks.

The claim cycle shortened for a related reason: when the visit is already logged next to the claim, the approver has less to chase [confirm with the client].

RESULTS
Daily visit logging: from 41% of reps to 93% of reps, in 10 weeks. In headcount, about 49 reps a day to about 112 of 120, so nearly the whole team now shows up in the day's data.
Expense-claim processing: from 9 days to 3 days, by the end of the same 10 weeks [confirm period with the client]. A rep now waits a third as long to be paid back.
What changed in the picture: the rural beats, the ones most likely to fall out of the record, are now part of it. [Name] can read coverage by beat instead of guessing from a weekly total.

Source: [Product] visit logs and [Distributor name]'s expense records, [month, year]. Logging rate means the share of the 120 reps with at least one visit logged on a working day [confirm definition]. There was no control group. The figures show what happened during the rollout, not how much of it other changes at the distributor explain.

"For a long time we ran on whatever reps remembered to tell us. Now 93 of every 100 log their day, and a claim that took nine days clears in three."
[Name], Head of Sales, [Distributor name] [draft wording: replace with the approved quote before publishing]

If your reps work patchy-network beats and your visit data has gaps, book a 20-minute demo: [link]. Bring your current daily logging rate and we will show you where offline mode and claim tracking would move it.

H1
Cotton Chikankari Kurtas for Women

INTRO (above the grid)
Cotton chikankari kurtas for women, hand-embroidered in Lucknow in white, pastel and festive colours. The cotton stays light in a hot office and the embroidery is soft enough for all-day wear, so one kurta can work at your desk and at the Diwali dinner. Filter by size, colour or occasion to see what fits you, or start with one of the collections below.

SUBCATEGORY LINKS
Chikankari kurtas for office wear [/collections/chikankari-kurtas-office]
Festive chikankari kurtas [/collections/chikankari-kurtas-festive]
White and pastel chikankari kurtas [/collections/white-pastel-chikankari-kurtas]
Mulmul chikankari kurtas for summer [/collections/mulmul-chikankari-kurtas]
Chikankari kurta sets with pants or palazzo [/collections/chikankari-kurta-sets]

BUYING GUIDE (below the grid)
How to choose a cotton chikankari kurta

Fabric
Cotton breathes and takes embroidery well, which is why it is the everyday base. Mulmul is the lightest and most sheer, good for peak summer and for wearing over a slip. A heavier cotton holds its shape through a working week and needs no lining. Check the fabric listed on each product page.

Fit and size
Use the size chart on the product page and compare bust, waist and hip with a kurta you already wear. Cotton can shrink slightly in the first wash, so if you are between two sizes, take the larger one. A straight cut looks sharp at work. An A-line moves better when you are dressed up and on your feet all evening.

Office or festive
For the office, choose white, pastel or muted shades with light work on the yoke and cuffs. For festive days, look for denser embroidery, such as jaali (net-like openwork) across the front, in deeper colours, and add a dupatta.

How to tell hand chikankari from machine chikan
Turn the kurta inside out. On hand work, the back shows thread paths and small knots, and the stitches are close but not identical. Bakhiya (shadow work) is stitched from the back, so you see a criss-cross of thread behind the fabric and a soft shadow on the front. Machine embroidery looks flat and exact, with every motif repeated the same way. Hand work costs more because each kurta is stitched slowly, by one person at a time.

Care
Hand wash in cold water with a mild detergent. Do not wring or scrub the embroidery. Wash dark colours separately the first time. Dry in shade and iron on the reverse side.

FAQ
Which size should I order?
Compare your bust, waist and hip with the size chart on the product page. Cotton can shrink a little after the first wash, so choose the larger size if you are between two.

Can I wear a chikankari kurta to the office?
Yes. Pick a straight cut in white, pastel or a muted colour with light work on the yoke. Keep dense jaali work for festive days.

Why do hand-embroidered kurtas cost more than machine-made ones?
Every kurta is embroidered by hand, stitch by stitch, and denser work takes longer. Machine embroidery is faster, which is why it is cheaper.

Will the embroidery get damaged in the wash?
Not if you hand wash it in cold water, do not wring it and dry it in shade. Wash dark colours on their own the first time.

GUDDU MISHRA
Guddu Mishra, 34, a Varanasi ghat boatman who hates being watched, goes viral on a stranger's phone and must ask a crowd for help to buy his own boat.

WANT, NEED, WOUND
Guddu wants a boat of his own. He rents one from Bhola Seth, pays daily rent whether he gets passengers or not, and keeps every rupee in a school notebook with a rubber band round it. The number he is saving towards is written on the cover, and he has never said it aloud.

He needs to be seen, and to let someone help him. He resists both.

The wound is his father's boat. When Guddu was 19, his father sold the family boat to cover his sister's wedding and told nobody the price. Guddu found out from the buyer. Since then he treats help as a debt and attention as a trap: whoever claims to be helping him is about to take something.

BEHAVIOUR AND FLAW
Under pressure Guddu gets quiet and rows harder. When a tourist haggles, he stops talking and takes the oars. He answers a ringing phone on the fourth ring, never the first. He fixes his own oarlocks, will not borrow a tool, and returns every borrowed cup of tea by buying the next one.

His flaw is pride, and it costs him money: he quotes tourists a fair fare, hears an argument, then drops the price just to end the conversation, and spends the evening angry at himself. He has never said "sorry" to his mother. He says "chalo."

VOICE
Hindi with Banarasi turns of phrase ("guru", "ई", "का हो"), short sentences, nearly no English except the numbers he needs for fares. He talks to oars and engines the way others talk to people. He never gives the price first, and he never says "please."

"कैमरा बाद में, पहले किराया तय करो, गुरु।" (Camera later, settle the fare first, guru.)
"हम नाव चलाते हैं, तमाशा नहीं।" (I row boats. I don't put on shows.)
"चलो, एक बार बोल देते हैं। बस एक बार।" (Fine, I'll say it once. Just once.)

LOOK (fixed visual block, reuse word for word)
Guddu Mishra, 34, lean and wiry, 5 ft 8 in, sun-darkened wheatish-brown skin, deep-set dark eyes, three-day stubble with early grey at the chin, short black hair thinning at the front, under a faded saffron-orange gamchha knotted at the head. A healed scar cuts through his left eyebrow and a crescent-shaped rope scar marks his right palm. He wears a faded sky-blue half-sleeve shirt, khaki trousers rolled to the calf, rubber slippers and a thin red moli thread on his right wrist. He carries a school notebook tucked into his waistband and a scratched phone in a cracked clear case.

RELATIONSHIPS
Sulochana Mishra, his mother: wants him married and safe, and keeps asking about the notebook.
Pintu, 12, his nephew: wants his uncle to be famous, and is the one who posts the first clip.
Bhola Seth, the boat owner: wants his rent on time, and wants Guddu quiet about the rate.
Tara Kapoor, a Delhi travel vlogger: filmed the clip that spreads, and wants Guddu on camera again for her next video.

ARC
Episode 1: Guddu counts every rupee and every word, and trusts neither a camera nor a kind offer. Episode 7 is the turn: a brand offers to buy him a boat if he stages his father's story for its ad. He says no, loses the boat, and tells the true story on camera, for free. By episode 10 he is still renting, still counting, and no longer rowing alone.

MISHTI AND THE THUNDER DRUM
Picture-book text for ages 3 to 6

SPREAD 1
Mishti lived in a para in Kolkata, where the monsoon came every year, loud and uninvited.
She loved the puddles. She loved paper boats.
She did not love the thunder.
Thakuma said the sky was only washing its face.
Mishti thought it could wash it more quietly.
Mishti wanted the rain, without the BOOM.

SPREAD 2
One afternoon the sky turned the colour of an old steel pot.
Mishti was folding a paper boat. Thakuma was fast asleep.
Gur-gur-gur... BOOM!
Mishti's tummy went thump.

SPREAD 3
So Mishti hid under the bed.
It was dusty. It was dark. It was very, very quiet.
Gur-gur-gur... BOOM!
The floor shook. The thunder had found her.
[The cat is already under there.]

SPREAD 4
So Mishti put her fingers in her ears and hummed her loudest hum, the tram-bell song.
Hmmmmmmm.
Gur-gur-gur... BOOM!
Louder than the hum. Louder than anything.

SPREAD 5
So Mishti marched to the window and shouted at the sky.
"Stop that," said Mishti.
"STOP THAT."
Gur-gur-gur... BOOM! BOOM!
The sky was not a good listener.

SPREAD 6
Mishti sat on the floor, small as a button.
The rain drummed on the roof. The thunder rolled down the whole para, right over her head.
Gur-gur-gur...
Mishti squeezed her eyes shut.
And in the dark behind her eyes, she heard it differently.
Rolling. Booming. Dhum. Dhum. Dhum.
She knew that sound.

SPREAD 7
It was a dhaak.
The very same sound the drummers made last Durga Puja, when Mishti danced all the way down the lane.
The sky was not angry.
The sky was practising.

SPREAD 8
Mishti ran to the kitchen.
She stood on her toes and took down the biggest steel pot. She took two wooden spoons.
Nobody helped her. Nobody had to.

SPREAD 9
Gur-gur-gur... BOOM!
"Dhum," said Mishti, and she hit the pot.
It was a small sound. But it was hers.
Her tummy still went thump. But now her hands went dhum.

SPREAD 10
Gur-gur-gur... BOOM!
"Dhum-dhum," said Mishti, much louder.
The cat came out from under the bed to listen.
His ears went up. His tail went up too.

SPREAD 11
Gur-gur-gur... BOOM!
"DHUM-DHUM-DHUM," said Mishti, louder than a tram.
The sky went one way. Mishti went the other. Back and forth, back and forth.
The sky was not winning.

SPREAD 12
Thakuma woke up.
Mishti did not stop. The sky did not stop.
Thakuma found Mishti in the middle of the room, drumming on her best pot.
Thakuma opened her mouth. Then she closed it. Then she fetched the lid and joined in.

SPREAD 13
The rain got softer. The puddles in the lane stopped shivering.
The thunder grumbled off towards Howrah.
Gur... gur... gur...
Far away. Very far.

SPREAD 14
Mishti still loved the puddles. She still loved paper boats.
And the BOOM? She wanted that too, just a little.
Gur-gur-gur... went the sky.
"Dhum," said Mishti, and her tummy went dhum too.
Next time, she would bring a bigger spoon.
